title: Gastrointestinal Comprehensive Set 1: Regulatory Substance (Short Answer)

questions.prompt: Name the four "official" gastrointestinal hormones and the two requirements they must meet regarding their route of delivery to target cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Gastrin, cholecystokinin (CCK), secretin, and glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP). They must be secreted in response to a physiologic stimulus and be carried in the bloodstream to a distant site to produce a physiologic action.

questions.prompt: Which cells secrete gastrin, and where are they primarily located?
questions.modelAnswer: G cells, located in the antrum of the stomach.

questions.prompt: What are the two major physiological actions of gastrin on the stomach?
questions.modelAnswer: It stimulates H^+ secretion by gastric parietal cells and stimulates the growth of the gastric mucosa (trophic effect).

questions.prompt: Identify the three primary stimuli that trigger the release of gastrin in response to a meal.
questions.modelAnswer: Small peptides and amino acids (especially phenylalanine and tryptophan), distention of the stomach, and vagal stimulation (via GRP).

questions.prompt: Explain the negative feedback mechanism that inhibits gastrin secretion.
questions.modelAnswer: Gastrin secretion is inhibited by a low pH (< 3.0) in the gastric lumen and by the paracrine somatostatin.

questions.prompt: Which cells synthesize and secrete cholecystokinin (CCK), and what specific triggers in the intestinal lumen stimulate its release?
questions.modelAnswer: I cells of the duodenum and jejunum. It is released in response to monoglycerides, fatty acids, small peptides, and amino acids.

questions.prompt: Describe the coordinated effect of CCK on the gallbladder and the sphincter of Oddi.
questions.modelAnswer: CCK stimulates the contraction of the gallbladder while simultaneously causing the relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi to eject bile into the duodenum.

questions.prompt: Aside from its effects on the biliary system, what are the three other major actions of CCK?
questions.modelAnswer: It stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, stimulates growth of the exocrine pancreas/gallbladder, and inhibits gastric emptying.

questions.prompt: What is the primary stimulus for the release of secretin, and what is its major function?
questions.modelAnswer: H^+ (acid) in the lumen of the duodenum. Its major function is to promote the secretion of pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate to neutralize that acid.

questions.prompt: How does secretin affect the pancreas and the liver to facilitate its primary function?
questions.modelAnswer: It stimulates pancreatic HCO_3^- secretion and increases HCO_3^- and H_2O secretion by the liver (bile production).

questions.prompt: Which gastrointestinal hormone is the only one released in response to all three major nutrients (glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids)?
questions.modelAnswer: Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP).

questions.prompt: Explain the "incretin" effect of glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP).
questions.modelAnswer: It stimulates insulin release from pancreatic beta cells in the presence of an oral glucose load.

questions.prompt: Which candidate hormone is responsible for initiating the migrating myoelectric complexes (MMCs) every 90 minutes during the interdigestive state?
questions.modelAnswer: Motilin.

questions.prompt: Identify the gastrointestinal paracrine that is released in response to decreased luminal pH and acts to inhibit the release of all GI hormones.
questions.modelAnswer: Somatostatin.

questions.prompt: Which paracrine substance is secreted by enteroendocrine-like cells of the gastric mucosa to increase H^+ secretion?
questions.modelAnswer: Histamine.

questions.prompt: Name the neurocrine released from parasympathetic postganglionic neurons that mediates the relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter.
questions.modelAnswer: Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).

questions.prompt: What is the function of gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP), and which nerves release it?
questions.modelAnswer: It is released from vagal neurons to stimulate gastrin release from G cells.

questions.prompt: Where are the satiety and feeding centers located in the brain?
questions.modelAnswer: The satiety center is in the ventromedial nucleus (or VPN), and the feeding center is in the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA).

questions.prompt: Contrast the roles of the arcuate nucleus neurons that release pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) versus those that release neuropeptide Y.
questions.modelAnswer: Anorexigenic neurons release POMC to decrease appetite, while orexigenic neurons release neuropeptide Y to increase appetite.

questions.prompt: Where is leptin produced, and how does its secretion correlate with body fat levels?
questions.modelAnswer: It is secreted by fat (adipose) cells in proportion to the amount of fat stored in the tissue.

questions.prompt: Which gastric hormone is secreted just before a meal to stimulate orexigenic neurons and increase appetite?
questions.modelAnswer: Ghrelin.

questions.prompt: What is the role of Peptide YY (PYY) in the regulation of food intake, and when is it released?
questions.modelAnswer: PYY is released from the small and large intestine following a meal to decrease appetite and food intake.

questions.prompt: Describe the mechanism by which insulin acts as a satiety signal.
questions.modelAnswer: Insulin (like leptin) stimulates anorexigenic neurons and inhibits orexigenic neurons in the arcuate nucleus to decrease appetite.

questions.prompt: How do GLP-1 and GIP differ from other GI hormones in their effect on the endocrine pancreas?
questions.modelAnswer: They are incretins, meaning they specifically promote the secretion of insulin in response to oral glucose.

questions.prompt: Which neurocrine is cosecreted with acetylcholine in the parasympathetic nerves to the salivary glands to cause vasodilation?
questions.modelAnswer: Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).
